newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD takes Waigel to court on 1996 budget.
newsitem.headline: SPD takes Waigel to court on 1996 budget.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Wednesday they would bring a case before the country's constitutional court alleging Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1996 budget was illegal.

The suit seeks a retroactive judgment from the court that the budget broke several articles of Germany's basic law -- in particular the fiscal "golden rule" which demands that the federal deficit does not exceed government investment.

Although a ruling may take years, the SPD said it wanted to put pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition not to resort to any further fiscal trickery to meet borrowing targets for Europe's single currency.
"We must step on the emergency brake," SPD finance policy spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier told a news conference.
The suit argues the government knew full well it would not adhere to the golden rule, enshrined in Article 115 of the constitution, when it drafted the 1996 federal budget.
The budget set a federal deficit of 58.8 billion marks ($34 billion) and investment at 66.3 billion marks.
In the end, a blowout in the social security budget -- which the SPD said was foreseeable -- forced up the deficit to 78.3 billion marks while investment fell short at 61 billion.

Under the constitution, such a deficit is only allowed to "prevent a loss of overall economic balance" -- effectively requiring a humiliating admission by the government it has lost control of the economy.
The Finance Ministry has argued that the constitution only refers to the budget's drafting, and not to its execution, and that the SPD case thus has no legal basis.

But the SPD case also argues the 1996 budget was drafted in the full knowledge that planned privatisation receipts of nine billion marks -- including still-unsold stakes in Postbank and airline Lufthansa AG -- could not be realised.

The SPD also argues that the constitution requires the government to pass a supplementary budget as soon as it becomes clear that the deficit will overshoot. By failing to do so, the government violated the rights of parliament, it states.

"The government consistently overrides basic budgetary and constitutional principles," Matthaeus-Maier said. "By now everyone knows that the Kohl government's budgets are not worth the paper they are written on even when they are passed."

The SPD legal action drew a quick rebuke from the budget spokesman of Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU/CSU) parliamentary faction. "It is simply a diversion from the SPD's own financial incapacity," Adolf Roth said in a statement.
"The case brought by the SPD will fail. A party which when in government was almost never able to announce a budget on time, won't win any credibility by going to court," Roth added.

There is a precedent for the case: Kohl, as leader of the German opposition, brought a case against the 1981 budget of Chancellor Helmut Schmidt's SPD-led coalition. The constitutional court threw out the suit in 1989.

Separately, CDU/CSU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble conceded on Wednesday that new borrowing may exceed investment under a supplementary budget for 1997 which the cabinet is due to adopt on July 11.

But, in an interview to be aired by ZDF television later on Wednesday, he said that the budget for 1998 which is also being drafted must conform to Article 115 of the constitution. ($ = 1.744 German Marks)
